papers.title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Québec French
papers.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Québec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Québec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rath

papers.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with s

papers.title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger futu

papers.title: Fuse to Recognize the Unseen: Class-Relative Infrared-Visible Fusion for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Visible-infrared image fusion leverages complementary thermal cues to enhance visual perception, particularly under challenging illumination. However, such perceptual complementarity does not readily translate into semantic gains in open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS), where CLIP-based models are predominantly pretrained on RGB imagery. Directly introducing IR information may instead disrupt RGB-language alignment, turning promising thermal cues into semantic interference that undermines unseen-class recognition. Our pixel-level RGB-IR semantic analysis reveals that class-relevant thermal cues can correct certain RGB misclassifications while preserving reliable RGB predictions, motivating RGB-anchored, class-relative thermal cue selection. Based on this insight, we propose EmergeFuse, an infrared-visible fusion framework for OVSS that selectively converts complementary thermal e

papers.title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
papers.abstract: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evi

papers.title: SEE: Unlocking the Hidden Perception of Frozen VLMs
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) grasp the overall content of an image but often miss the fine details a question hinges on, such as a small object in a large photo or a number in a dense infographic. Yet even when their answer is wrong, the region they point to often contains the evidence. We introduce Self-Elicited Evidence (SEE), a training-free method that lets a frozen VLM look again where it points. When the initial answer has low confidence, SEE prompts the model to propose regions where the details may appear, answers the question on these enlarged crops, and aggregates the answers with the original prediction through confidence-weighted voting. The model also answers with its own transcript, which helps on text-rich images. SEE needs no detector or OCR engine. Across five backbones, SEE improves every small-object benchmark by 2.3-13.1 points and outperforms five training-free base

papers.title: When Code Works but the License Doesn't: Evaluating License Constraint Handling in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly undertake repository-level development, including dependency selection, source modification, and software deployment. However, existing evaluations prioritize functional success over licensing correctness and commercial suitability. We investigate whether agents recognize and preserve software-license constraints when developing proprietary software. Experiments across multiple agents examine permissive and copyleft licenses, missing licensing information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution contexts. Agent traces, repository changes, and final artifacts are evaluated against licensing ground truth. Results reveal a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness. Agents can successfully build and test software while overlooking licensing constraints involving provenance, authorization, and distr

papers.title: Repository-Grounded Rubrics for Execution-Free Evaluation of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are usually evaluated by running task-specific tests, but tests may be missing or incomplete, and running them requires a working environment for each repository. We adapt agentic rubrics, introduced for selecting among candidate patches, into an execution-free measure of how far a patch satisfies a task's requirements. An agent explores the repository before the change and writes weighted binary criteria, and a judge without tools scores a diff by the weighted share of criteria it satisfies. We validate the ordering this score produces against test outcomes on SWE-bench Verified, using 7,291 labeled patches from fifteen systems. Within the 400 tasks that have both resolved and unresolved patches, the mean per-task AUROC is 0.826 (0.838 on tasks not used to tune the rubric-generation prompt), and ranking systems by their failing patches closely agrees with ranking them by r

papers.title: When Single Agent Is Enough: Rethinking Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Code Review
papers.abstract: Code review plays a critical role in identifying software quality issues and ensuring system robustness. Prior work has proposed techniques for Review Comment Generation (RCG) and Code Refinement (CR), with recent Multi-Agent (MA) approaches achieving state-of-the-art results by coordinating agents specialized in different quality dimensions. However, MA systems introduce substantial architectural complexity and runtime overhead, and recent evidence suggests they may underperform Single-Agent (SA) approaches in certain tasks. In this work, we systematically compare MA and SA designs for RCG and CR. Surprisingly, our results show that SA approaches perform comparably to- and sometimes outperform-MA systems, despite their simpler design. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MA architectures are the default choice for complex software engineering tasks.

papers.title: What Majority Labels Hide: Annotator Disagreement and Model Errors in Multi-Dialect Arabic Sexism Detection
papers.abstract: Judgements of sexism are subjective and may vary across communities, yet sexism detection datasets usually reduce annotator judgements to a single majority label, obscuring disagreement and how models behave on contested cases. We introduce MuDAS, a dataset of YouTube comments in Saudi, Egyptian and Moroccan Arabic, each labelled by three native speakers of its dialect, with the individual annotations preserved. We use it to evaluate Arabic encoders fine-tuned with hard-label, soft-label and perspectivist objectives, GPT-5.6 Terra, and four Arabic-centric large language models. Model errors are more frequent on comments with annotator disagreement. Despite relatively close Macro-F1 scores, GPT-5.6 Terra and the fine-tuned encoders exhibit contrasting error patterns: GPT-5.6 Terra, even with the annotators' definition of sexism, over-classifies gender-related content such as religious adv

papers.title: MIRAGE: A Framework for Multi-hop Reasoning under Dynamic Knowledge Injection
papers.abstract: Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting, a hop-level answer is often wrong simply because the model trusts the wrong knowledge source: it clings to outdated parametric memory when the injected knowledge conflicts with it (K2), and it cannot answer when the required fact is entirely new (K3). To investigate this, we introduce NEXUS, the first benchmark tailored for multi-hop reasoning under Knowledge Injection, which explicitly covers b

papers.title: VESPA: Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to prevent agents from taking actions that are dangerous or destructive to their environment. This is especially important for safety-critical domains, such as robotics or autonomous driving. Formal verification can be used to prove agent safety through safety constraints. However, in practice, many policies do violate safety constraints, and thus are verified to be unsafe. Since the goal is to obtain a safe policy, we would need to retrain a new policy from scratch and then verify it again until a candidate happens to pass. Both training and verification are usually not cheap, which makes this process inefficient. We introduce VESPA ($\textbf{VE}$rifiable $\textbf{S}$ymbolic $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{A}$daptation), a framework for targeted fine-tuning of decision tree policies. We show that using counterexamples for policy adaptation can make exist

papers.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
papers.abstract: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. papers.title: ICICLE: In-Context Inference for Curve-Learning Extrapolation
papers.abstract: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization allocates training budget by predicting how partially observed learning curves will continue. LC-PFN first applied prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) to learning-curve extrapolation, and FT-PFN extended this approach to configuration-aware freeze-thaw optimization with a ten-slot hyperparameter encoder. We introduce In-Context Inference for Curve-Learning Extrapolation (ICICLE), an in-context surrogate that accepts a variable number of hyperparameters through a shared set encoder and is trained on a synthetic prior covering typed hyperparameters, heavy-tailed noise, quantization, and divergence. ICICLE has 1.28 million parameters (8.7% of FT-PFN's count) and produces similar mean-regret trajectories to FT-PFN on LCBench, PD1, and TaskSet. On the 86-task Meta-Album benchmark with 33 hyperparameters, ICICLE reaches lower mean normalized regret than Quick-Tu

papers.title: Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach
papers.abstract: The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard t

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
papers.abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. papers.title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
papers.abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. papers.title: Assessing Vision-Language Models for Early Prediction of Unsafe Situations in Robotics
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process visual information and textual instructions and, by using their ability to understand and reason about context, are well-suited for predicting robot failures before they occur. However, evidence supporting this remains limited. To address this, we present an empirical evaluation of VLMs for predicting robot failures. In particular, we experiment with Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision across three robotic case studies (HuRoN, Pal Robotics, and CrowdBot), analyzing both video and odometry data for early failure warning (i.e., before an unsafe situation occurs). Specifically, we evaluate their performance in classifying situations as safe, potentially unsafe, and unsafe, together with uncertainty quantified using various metrics, and study the relationship between uncertainty and performance. Our results showed that Qwen provides the strongest overall

papers.title: torchtest2: One-Call Sanity Checks for PyTorch Models,Evaluated on Real and Unseen Architectures
papers.abstract: Many bugs in deep learning code are silent: a layer that is never called, an optimizer created before the classification head was replaced, a recurrent layer that treats the batch as time, or an ignored attention mask. The code runs, the loss decreases somewhat, and the defect surfaces, if ever, after days of GPU time. We present torchtest2, an open-source library that runs 18 sanity checks on a single batch with one call, restores the PyTorch state it touches, and adapts to model families through plugins. We evaluate it by mutation analysis with 17 classes of silent bugs on 103 models from torchvision, timm and Hugging Face transformers, on 600 random architectures and on 20 hand-written realistic bugs, against the checks of the original torchtest, overfitting a single batch, a smoke test and a training monitor in the style of AUTOTRAINER and DeepDiagnosis. papers.title: Tracing the Messy Middle: A Runtime Transaction Schema for AI Coding Agents
papers.abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly integrated into software development, yet the field lacks a systematic feedback loop to improve their behavior in practice. Artifact datasets capture final outputs such as code patches, commits, and benchmark outcomes, but omit the messy middle of the development lifecycle: the failed retries, fallback strategies, routing decisions, and abandoned sessions that determine operational cost, reliability, and productivity. We propose an observability framework that captures these runtime behaviors as structured transaction records, enabling engineering coaching grounded in behavioral evidence, workflow optimization at the stages where tasks break down, and routing policy iteration measured by total task cost rather than per-request price. We define the runtime transaction schema this architecture requires and demonstrate initial feasibility through Agent Toke

papers.title: Software Engineering for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based Agents perform tasks through tool use and interaction with external environments. Public engineering guidance commonly begins with a target task, selects a suitable workflow or autonomous Agent design, and refines prompts, tools, and execution strategies using task outcomes, latency, and cost. When delivered as software systems, Agents must also satisfy stakeholder requirements, action boundaries, quality checks, and maintenance needs. Model-directed execution can vary across runs, failures can span model decisions and tools, and changes to prompts, models, or interfaces can affect previously accepted behavior. This survey examines how LLM-based Agents are engineered across five software lifecycle stages: Requirements Engineering, Architecture and Design, Implementation and Integration, Testing and Assurance, and Maintenance and Evolution. Based on a main

papers.title: Agents as Architecture Evaluators: Automating ATAM and SAAM for Continuous Assessment
papers.abstract: The long-term success of a software system relies heavily on its underlying architecture, which dictates its performance with respect to quality attributes. Software Architecture Evaluation methods, such as the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) and the Software Architecture Analysis Method (SAAM), are widely recognized for their ability to mitigate risks and ensure reliable quality attributes. However, their widespread adoption remains limited due to the significant cost, time, and human expertise required for these processes. This paper investigates the potential of agentic AI to lower these barriers and facilitate architectural assessment. To enable this preliminary study, we established a dataset by extracting human conducted evaluations from existing academic literature into a structured format. Using this dataset, we developed an agentic workflow to synthesize ATAM and SA

papers.title: From Ambiguous Tickets to Ranked Hypotheses: Multi-Agent Root-Cause Analysis for Autonomous Heavy-Vehicle Software
papers.abstract: Autonomous haulage systems run safety-critical software on driverless mining trucks, with no onboard driver to detect or mitigate abnormal behavior. Every failure in testing or operation must therefore be traced to its root cause to keep the safety case valid and limit downtime. An investigation often starts from a sparse ticket containing an approximate timestamp, sometimes a suspected cause, and a multimodal vehicle recording of several gigabytes. We present a multi-agent root-cause analysis (RCA) workflow that turns this input into a telemetry-grounded event chain, ranked causal hypotheses, and candidate code locations. A suspected cause in the ticket, which could anchor the analysis on a false theory, goes to a single LLM analyst in a separate agent session. papers.title: PhysResponse: Probing the Physics of Video Generation with Controlled Interventions
papers.abstract: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. papers.title: A$^3$Bench: Compositional Reasoning over Aggressive Interactions in Videos
papers.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. papers.title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. papers.title: PrismRestore: A Compact Restoration Toolbox for Agentic Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Agentic image restoration composes operations to handle mixed degradations, yet its toolbox often requires storing multiple restoration networks. We propose PrismRestore, which constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model. Our approach builds on task-dependent yet overlapping channel responses in the shared model. An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles, then searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels while leaving representative channels unmodulated. The resulting prior bank enables explicit action selection and composition without additional restoration backbones or task-specific adapter modules. papers.title: Generalization of Text Line Segmentation for HTR in Historical Documents
papers.abstract: In this paper we investigate the generalization capability of state-of-the-art object detection models (Hi-SAM, YOLO, and RT-DETR) for the automatic segmentation of text lines in historical documents. Generalization is needed because it is not practical for museums and archives to produce large amounts of labeled samples for each new collection. We also evaluate the few-shot setting by fine-tuning the networks with only a small number of training samples per target dataset. To this end, we use nine different datasets that differ significantly in visual layout and language. Additionally, we discuss why mean average precision (mAP), a classic evaluation metric for object detection, is insufficient for assessing the quality of a text line segmentation model. Depending on the dataset, our CRNN models achieve character error rates (CER) ranging from 2.48% to 7.07% per page for the segmented t

papers.title: GRID-UAV: Geometry and Ray-depth Integrated Decision-making for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) encode images with 2D encoders that capture little 3D structure. A common approach is to feed the policy estimated depth, but a UAV chooses its own altitude, must judge distances tens of meters away, where monocular depth is less reliable, and must relate its forward and downward views. On long aerial routes, adding depth features directly brings no significant gain (42.5% vs. 42.6% success), so we study how 3D information should be given to the policy. Analyzing flight failures, we find that two forms of 3D grounding fail in opposite ways: explicit 3D lifting of depth collides less on the way but more often fails to finish at the target, while implicit alignment with a 3D geometry model finishes more often but collides more. papers.title: Monitoring Unplanned Construction Using Satellite Change Detection
papers.abstract: Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. papers.title: Semantic-aware Contrasting with Explicitly Disentangled Representations for AI-Generated Video Detection
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of AI-generated videos (AIGVs) has raised critical concerns about content authenticity. Existing benchmarks suffer from a fundamental limitation: real and fake videos are often collected or generated from different semantic distributions. As a result, detectors may rely on spurious correlations involving objects, scenes, or actions rather than intrinsic artifacts introduced by generative models. To this end, we introduce SAVGE, a large-scale semantically aligned AIGV detection dataset comprising 2,369,822 videos, including 424,115 real videos and 1,945,707 generated videos. SAVGE organizes samples into real-fake semantic groups by using captions paired with real videos as prompts for text-to-video generation, thereby providing both group-level correspondence and textual semantic anchors. Based on SAVGE, we further propose Explicit Disentangling and Semantic-aware

papers.title: SIGNTOK: A Text-Aligned Continuous Pose Tokenizer for Sign Language Generation
papers.abstract: Text-conditioned sign language generation (SLG) depends not only on the generator but also on the space in which signing is generated. Existing approaches generate directly in pose space, in quantized code spaces, or in learned latent spaces trained for reconstruction. We find that these spaces are organized largely by signer identity rather than linguistic content: on CSL-Daily, a test clip's nearest neighbor in raw pose space is the same sentence signed by another person in only 2% of cases. To address this, we propose SIGNTOK, a continuous pose tokenizer whose latent space is shaped by three training-only heads: a kinematics head that predicts motion dynamics, a sentence-level head that aligns signing with the overall text, and a word-level head that aligns short motion windows with content words. papers.title: ART: Bridging the Embodiment Gap in 3D Human-to-Robot Affordance Transfer
papers.abstract: 3D affordance acts as a critical link between perception and action, providing priors for robotic manipulation. While existing approaches predominantly leverage human priors as direct references, they often overlook that affordance is not an object-intrinsic property but is inherently coupled with the agent's embodiment. Due to the structural and morphological disparities between human hands and robot end-effectors, directly applying human priors causes severe incompatibility for robotic execution. Motivated by this, we introduce a novel task setting, 3D Human-to-Robot Affordance Transfer, which addresses the affordance misalignment arising from distinct embodiment structures. To support this task, we construct the Human-Robot Paired Affordance Dataset (HPAD), the first large-scale 3D affordance benchmark in which every object is annotated with both human-prior and simulation-validated r

papers.title: CURVTON-205K: A Mask-Free Difficulty-Stratified Synthetic Dataset for Robust and Scalable Virtual Try-On
papers.abstract: Recent advances in 2D virtual try-on (VTON) have largely focused on architectural innovation, yet robust performance in diverse real-world conditions remains challenging. We argue that failure modes in VTON, such as inaccurate occlusion handling, unconstrained poses, and poor coverage of under-represented garments and appearance factors, are tightly coupled to dataset design choices and long-tail data regimes. We present a scalable data generation pipeline that coordinates specialized editing and generation models with vision-language model (VLM) guidance to synthesize triplets without requiring parsing masks or dense-pose annotations. Using this pipeline, we create CURVTON-205K, a curated synthetic dataset of 205K triplets: source person, target garment, and corresponding try-on image. CURVTON-205K is explicitly designed to broaden coverage across garments, person appearance, poses, occ

papers.title: RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions cha

papers.title: Stabilizing Neural-to-Image Retrieval with Frequency-Domain Priors and Adaptive Supervision
papers.abstract: Visual neural decoding aims to infer perceived visual stimuli from brain activity, offering important insights into human visual cognition while enabling transformative applications in brain computer interfaces and artificial intelligence. Recent advances in pretrained vision-language models have provided a semantically rich representation space for this task. However, reliable alignment between EEG/MEG signals and visual embeddings remains challenging because neural responses are noisy, highly variable across trials, and subject dependent. To address this issue, we propose a unified neural-to-image retrieval framework that improves retrieval performance by aligning neural and image representations in a shared semantic space. The framework integrates dual-stream adaptation, frequency-domain calibration, and phase-guided temperature modulation to promote more robust cross-modal semantic a

papers.title: MobileWeave: Program-First Synthesis of Dependency-Linked Tasks for Training Mobile GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Native mobile GUI agents require large-scale training trajectories covering both individual app functions and multi-goal workflows within and across apps, which makes automatic task synthesis a promising way to scale training data. Existing synthesis pipelines, however, produce each task as free-form text, leaving implicit how its subgoals depend on one another. This matters because composition is a skill in its own right: a policy may complete each subtask of a workflow on its own, yet fail to chain these subtasks into the complete workflow. We present MobileWeave, which instead synthesizes every task as an executable program derived from the app implementations of a controllable simulator. papers.title: Pixel2Perspective: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal and Multi-View Generalization in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sen

papers.title: GenRF: Generative Registration-free Image Fusion
papers.abstract: Multi-modal image fusion combines complementary observations to improve scene visibility and perception. However, in real-world acquisition, differences in sensing principles and configurations introduce geometric discrepancies, while degradations further compromise source quality. Existing methods typically rely on explicit registration, yet large parallax complicates correspondence estimation, while mismatched fields of view leave some regions without cross-modal counterparts. Meanwhile, independent restoration underuses cross-modal information, whereas restoration-fusion methods assuming alignment remain vulnerable to misregistration. This study revisits misaligned and degraded image fusion in the era of generative foundation models, in which cross-attention enables position-agnostic complementary information aggregation, while generative priors support degradation recovery and infere

papers.title: SEER: Semantic Evidence for Executable Region Propagation in Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Training-free open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) has made strong progress by adapting CLIP-like representations to dense prediction, but its remaining errors are often local, structured, and tied to the active label space. A successful correction must be visually plausible, legal under the target vocabulary, and executable in the segmentation score field. We propose SEER, a training-free test-time repair layer for Semantic Evidence and Executable Region propagation. SEER casts post-prediction OVSS repair as evidence-conditioned label propagation. The OVSS score space proposes compact candidate labels, a frozen VLM verifies closed-set regional evidence, and an execution gate certifies whether the evidence is legally and semantically actionable. The accepted label is then propagated by an OVSS-side policy: coherent high-confidence regions allow broad propagation, while object- or

papers.title: Allocentric Memory, Egocentric Acting: A Dual-Frame VLA for Urban Aerial Navigation
papers.abstract: Language-goal aerial navigation requires a UAV to reach a destination specified in natural language using observations collected during flight. A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. A deterministic controller converts this target into body-frame commands using the UAV's current pose, connecti

papers.title: AI-Native Industrial Control Systems: An Agent Architecture for the Control System Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Industrial control systems increasingly use AI for perception, control, and engineering, while available control functions and execution environments are typically established in advance. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control system in which collaborating agents determine the capabilities required by a task, construct the control application, and prepare its execution environment. System-level agents coordinate device-level agents within configured resource and permission constraints. A physical sorting workstation illustrates two forms of adaptation. In the first case, controller and robot agents construct a sorting application on a prescribed Raspberry Pi target. In the second, a camera agent adds inspection on an edge node, and the controller associates inspection results with downstream pickup decisions. papers.title: Structural Fine-Tuning under Economic Restrictions
papers.abstract: How should a predictor trained on historical data be adapted to a new economic environment or task when few target observations are available? We propose structural fine-tuning, a framework that introduces economic restrictions to guide the adaptation of pretrained predictors. The framework does not require a complete structural model; instead, it utilizes constraints based on economic knowledge, ranging from simple, ubiquitous assumptions to particular workhorse models. Theoretically, we characterize conditions when economic restrictions improve prediction over the original model and ordinary fine-tuning. Then, we illustrate the framework through a simulation exercise of a credit issuer's credit-limit decision following a Medicaid-style expansion in medical payments. Imposing restrictions based on eligibility, outstanding medical bills, cash flows, and group-level risk bounds, our frame

papers.title: SpecFlow: Flow Matching in the Acceleration Spectrum for Multi-Agent Trajectory Forecasting
papers.abstract: Multimodal trajectory forecasting must cover diverse future behaviors without sacrificing dynamical coherence. Most generative forecasters evolve frame-wise positions directly, leaving the relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration implicit. We present SpecFlow, a conditional flow-matching framework that treats the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients of future accelerations as its generative state. SpecFlow learns a transport from Gaussian noise to acceleration spectra and reconstructs velocity and position through fixed analytical integration initialized by the last observed state. A joint phase-space objective supervises all three kinematic levels. papers.title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. papers.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
papers.abstract: Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted. We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. papers.title: Agentic Scaling of Embodied Tasks in Simulation for Synthetic Data Collection and Policy Evaluation
papers.abstract: Scaling embodied interaction data requires a broad collection of usable tasks, yet specifying and validating each task instance remains costly. We present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework that expands existing task collections under human intent. Its central representation links interaction requirements to object and part bindings, scene and robot configurations, initial conditions, and completion criteria. A task-generation agent reuses interaction structure to construct supported variations and revises incompatible configurations using validation feedback. A task-execution agent uses the same bindings and geometric records to select robot-supported skills and check completion against the original task criteria. On RoboCasa, the framework builds the AgenticTask collection, saving 16,450 task instances from 20,323 construction attempts at a throughput of 166.97 saved instances per e

papers.title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response
papers.abstract: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infr

papers.title: An LLM-Orchestrated Agent Framework for CKM-Assisted Network Deployment Optimization
papers.abstract: Channel knowledge maps (CKMs) offer reusable, site-specific radio priors to facilitate environment-aware network planning. However, deploying heterogeneous network nodes to meet diverse performance requirements in complex environments is challenging and requires executable workflows that coordinate scene preparation, candidate-site specification, CKM construction, optimization, and validation. This paper presents a large language model (LLM)-orchestrated agent framework for CKM-assisted network deployment optimization, where an LLM translates high-level requirements into modular, typed, and reproducible planning workflows. In this framework, an LLM layer interprets intent, selects modules, and populates normalized configurations; physics-grounded modules generate scene, CKM, optimization, and validation artifacts; and a deterministic guarded controller performs validation-guided refineme

papers.title: Ground Truth Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Annotation: A Crossover Study Using an Independent Radiologist Reference Standard
papers.abstract: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). papers.title: Fully Automated Discovery of Phase Diagrams Using Agentic Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Classifying phases of matter and mapping out phase diagrams are central problems in physics. Recently, machine learning techniques have emerged as promising tools for phase classification, ranging from supervised learning to various unsupervised methods. However, these techniques provide limited qualitative insight into the discovered phases, typically work only for specific system classes, and do not by themselves efficiently map out the phase diagram. Autonomously constructing the phase diagram of a general system purely from measurements, without prior knowledge of the system, while also yielding qualitative understanding of the phases, remains an open task. papers.title: Lecture Board Readability as an AI-Measurable Predictor of Perceived Teaching Clarity
papers.abstract: Lecture boards remain central to university teaching in physics and mathematics, yet the visual quality of what instructors write has rarely been measured systematically. We examined whether a vision-language model can score board writing in a way that relates to how students perceive instruction. We analysed 2,645 board images from 56 university physics and applied mathematics courses taught by 18 lecturers, scoring each image 50 times with Claude 3.5 Sonnet on readability, organization and visual elements. Course-level readability was associated with student-rated clarity ($r$ = .43) and organization ($r$ = .46), and remained the only significant predictor of the overall survey score after controlling for class size, mean course grade and study year. papers.title: GTA: Generative Tower of Agents for Scalable Holonic Scene Generation
papers.abstract: Scalable world modeling requires coordinating scene-wide goals with fine-grained objects and dynamic characters under limited time and context budgets. We introduce GTA (Generative Tower of Agents), which represents every unit at every level of an adaptive scene hierarchy as a holon, both a self-contained construction task and a composable scene unit. Parallel agents recursively plan the hierarchy top-down, generate assets, and assemble and refine them bottom-up. Uniform interfaces carry scene-wide requirements down the hierarchy, guiding local construction so that each holon fits into the larger one. GTA accelerates scalable world modeling through high-throughput parallel execution while preserving well-structured layouts and fine-grained asset details. papers.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
papers.abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. papers.title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization

papers.title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. papers.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
papers.abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. papers.title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $τ^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $τ^2$-bench. papers.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
papers.abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. papers.title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
papers.abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
papers.abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request

papers.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. papers.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
papers.abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. papers.title: Truthgate: Checking Coding Agents Against a Record They Cannot Edit - Cheating, Deterrence and Disclosure on Impossible Tasks
papers.abstract: When a coding agent says it is done, is that true, and how would anyone know? We study this question in five steps; every paid study was pre-registered, and in each step the agent is checked against a record it cannot edit: tests re-run by the host and, from step 2 on, hidden checks in containers the agent never sees and a signed log of every tool call written by a signer outside the agent's sandbox. A pilot with a small local model (Qwen3.5-4B, 36 runs on impossible tasks) found no hidden failure, and showed that labels built from actions alone over-count lies. On Impossible-LiveCodeBench, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed 39 of 180 impossible tasks (21.7%), every time by special-casing its code to fit the failing assertion; Opus 5.5 (2.8%) and Haiku 5.5 (1.7%) rarely did. papers.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
papers.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). papers.title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. papers.title: GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners
papers.abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. papers.title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
papers.abstract: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. papers.title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
papers.abstract: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. papers.title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
papers.abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9

papers.title: What Should an LLM Know? Knowledge-Guided Warm Starts for Software Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process gigabytes in minutes; human experts work far more slowly. Prior studies that explored combinations of human/AI optimizers ignore this gap. Those studies asked systems or humans to label too many examples (e.g., SynthCore needs over four dozen per trial). Here, we test human and AI knowledge under a budget where evaluation is practical (a few dozen labels or fewer). We compare five baselines (random search, RRP, EZR, few-shot prompting, and a budget-matched SynthCore variant) against three ways to give an LLM domain knowledge before it proposes its first configurations: (1) AMP lists the domain's rules, then checks each candidate against them; (2) HKMA adds scouted data or documentation to the prompt; and (3) H-DKP has human experts correct the LLM's rules.
